newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks nosedive despite yen's recovery.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks nosedive despite yen's recovery.

text.p: Japanese shares nosedived on Tuesday on jitters about the economy, drawing little strength from a comeback by the yen on currency markets.
Defying another record-breaking rally on Wall Street and the yen's advance against the dollar, the stock market's key Nikkei average fell a sharp 2.83 percent to its lowest close in more than a year.

On the foreign exchange market, the yen managed to push the dollar into retreat in early trade after Japanese monetary authorities, fearful of a flight from yen-based assets, warned of action to curb excessive currency swings.
The comments dampened down the dollar, pushing it below 115 yen at one point, but the despondency that clung to the stock market helped the greenback regain some ground by late trade.

The Nikkei 225 average closed below the key psychological level of 19,000 after hectic sales led by weakness on the futures market, shedding 549.81 points to close at 18,896.19. This was its lowest close since December 5, 1995.

The yen hovered at 115.30 to the dollar in late Tokyo trading against its New York close of around 115.77 to the dollar on Monday. The dollar had rallied to 117 yen, its highest level in almost four years, in Tokyo on Monday before the monetary authorities stepped in to check its ascent.

The yen's recovery on Tuesday, which would normally help the stock market by boosting the dollar value of yen-based assets, was not strong enough to convince investors that the currency trend has been reversed.
"I don't think the yen's downtrend will be halted only by verbal intervention," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.

"The yen's current weakness has been heightened by Japan's expected weak growth, as has that of stocks. Unless (Prime Minister Ryutaro) Hashimoto proposes something specific to shore up the economy, the situation will not change," he said.

Tokyo stock prices have been battered in recent sessions by worries that a planned rise in the sales tax and an end to special income tax cuts in April may choke off Japan's fragile economic recovery.
Analysts said stocks would continue to slide, possibly towards 18,500, if the government failed to come up with concrete measures to boost confidence.

The yen's recovery was sparked by a raft of comments from Japanese officials warning that they viewed an excessively weak yen as damaging for the economy and signalling they would act on foreign exchange markets to shore up the currency.
"An excessively weak or strong yen is not favourable for the Japanese economy," Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Tuesday.
"We want exchange rates to stabilise," he said.
Currency dealers said the dollar was unlikely to fall below 114.50 yen, where Japanese investors were expected to sell yen related to their fresh investments in foreign securities.

"For the time being I think they (Japanese officials) are succeeding in verbal intervention...so I think they may succeed at holding the dollar in a 114-116 yen range," said Chris Pavlou of Midland Bank Plc in Tokyo.
